claim: Varied numbers of 5C.C7 TCR Transgenic Rag2−/− T cells were cultured with I-Ek-expressing B10.A Cd3e−/− splenocytes pulsed with varied concentrations of K5 peptide.
source: Varied numbers (NTcell) of 5C.C7 TCR Transgenic Rag2−/− T cells were cultured in duplicate in 200 µl of complete medium with 5.105 I-Ek-expressing B10.A Cd3e−/−splenocytes pulsed with varied concentrations of K5 peptide ([Antigen]).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental setup from the manuscript text.

claim: T cells respond in a quantal manner to graded doses of antigen across various readouts including ERK phosphorylation, IL-2Rα expression, IL-2 expression, and cell cycle entrance.
source: These measurements demonstrate (A) the bimodality of T cell activation as well as (B) the limited dynamics range of response for varied doses of antigens.
evidence: Figure 1A shows bimodal distributions of activation markers, and the text explicitly states this demonstrates bimodality of T cell activation.

claim: A 1000-fold increase in antigen translated into at best a 50-fold gain in the IL-2 production response at single timepoints.
source: Increasing the stimulating dose of antigen for 100,000 T cells did amplify the frequency of activation, but not in proportion to the shift in input stimulus: several readouts were saturated for higher antigen doses, and at best, a 1000-fold increase in antigen translated into 50-fold gain in the IL-2 production response (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with reference to experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IL-2 accumulation at 12 hr was greatly influenced by the numbers of T cells in the system, with smaller populations demonstrating poorer antigen resolution.
source: IL-2 accumulation at 12 hr reflected this limited antigen-scaling in the frequency of IL-2 producers; furthermore, scaling at 12 hr was greatly influenced by the numbers of T cells in the system, with smaller populations demonstrating poorer antigen resolution (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with reference to Figure 1C data.

claim: IL-2 accumulated rapidly and non-linearly with time, then exponentially decreased.
source: However, probing further the IL-2 dynamics over days post-activation, we found that IL-2 accumulated rapidly and non-linearly with time, then exponentially decreased (Figure 2A–B,D), despite limited variation in the number of cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with reference to experimental data in Figures 2A-D.

claim: [IL-2]max is proportional to the T cell population's total [IL-2] accumulation over time.
source: For each condition, we characterized these dynamics by their apex, [IL-2]max, a quantity which was proportional to the T cell population's total [IL-2] accumulation over time (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 2E showing the correlation.

claim: [IL-2]max scaled as a power law that could distinguish more than three orders of magnitude of input antigen dose.
source: Strikingly, [IL-2]max scaled as a power law that could distinguish more than three orders of magnitude of input antigen dose (Figure 2F), despite the aforementioned saturated dynamic range of early T cell responses.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2F showing the power law relationship.

claim: [IL-2]max was essentially independent of the number of antigen-specific T cells in the culture.
source: Furthermore, [IL-2]max was essentially independent of the number of antigen-specific T cells in the culture (NT cells) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 2G showing independence from T cell numbers.

claim: 1000 T cells accumulated equal or greater amounts of IL-2 as 100-fold larger populations, in less than twice as much time.
source: Given the same stimulus, 1000 T cells accumulated equal or greater amounts of IL-2 as 100-fold larger populations, in less than twice as much time.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text describing the experimental observations.

claim: Changes in cell number through proliferation or death were at most two-fold by the time parity was gained in IL-2 accumulation.
source: This could not be accounted for by differential changes in cell number (through proliferation or death), which were at most two-fold by the time parity was gained in IL-2 accumulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 2C showing cell number changes.

claim: [IL-2]max scales with (NT cells)^(-0.10±0.02) × [Antigen]^(+0.76±0.05).
source: From 118 conditions over six independent experiments, we derived a simple empirical scaling law that summarizes the population size-independence and large scalability of IL-2 accumulation (Figure 2H):(1)[IL−2]maxexperiment∝(NT cells)−0.10(±0.02)×[Antigen]+0.76(±0.05).
evidence: This is the empirical scaling law explicitly stated and derived from 118 experimental conditions.

claim: T cells bimodally secrete IL-2 following TCR engagement.
source: It has been established that T cells bimodally secrete IL-2 (Podtschaske et al., 2007) and express the α chain of the IL-2 receptor (IL-2Rα) (Sheldon et al., 1993) following TCR engagement.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior literature.

claim: T cells express the α chain of the IL-2 receptor (IL-2Rα) following TCR engagement.
source: It has been established that T cells bimodally secrete IL-2 (Podtschaske et al., 2007) and express the α chain of the IL-2 receptor (IL-2Rα) (Sheldon et al., 1993) following TCR engagement.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Sheldon et al., 1993.

claim: IL-2 production is switched off after loss of TCR signaling.
source: IL-2 production is subsequently switched off after loss of TCR signaling (Huppa et al., 2003) and/or gain of IL-2 response via phosphorylation of the transcription factor STAT5 into pSTAT5 (Long and Adler, 2006; Villarino et al., 2007; Feinerman et al., 2010; Waysbort et al., 2013), which also mediates further upregulation of IL-2Rα (Smith and Cantrell, 1985; Waysbort et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Huppa et al., 2003.

claim: IL-2 production is switched off after gain of IL-2 response via phosphorylation of STAT5 into pSTAT5.
source: IL-2 production is subsequently switched off after loss of TCR signaling (Huppa et al., 2003) and/or gain of IL-2 response via phosphorylation of the transcription factor STAT5 into pSTAT5 (Long and Adler, 2006; Villarino et al., 2007; Feinerman et al., 2010; Waysbort et al., 2013), which also mediates further upregulation of IL-2Rα (Smith and Cantrell, 1985; Waysbort et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: pSTAT5 mediates upregulation of IL-2Rα.
source: IL-2 production is subsequently switched off after loss of TCR signaling (Huppa et al., 2003) and/or gain of IL-2 response via phosphorylation of the transcription factor STAT5 into pSTAT5 (Long and Adler, 2006; Villarino et al., 2007; Feinerman et al., 2010; Waysbort et al., 2013), which also mediates further upregulation of IL-2Rα (Smith and Cantrell, 1985; Waysbort et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Smith and Cantrell, 1985 and Waysbort et al., 2013.

claim: The classical model of IL-2 production predicted that T cells would accumulate IL-2 commensurably with the size of their population.
source: Implementation of this classical model (Figure 3B–E) predicted that T cells would accumulate IL-2 commensurably with the size of their population.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the computational model shown in Figure 3.

claim: The classical model of IL-2 production predicted a weak antigen dependency that saturated near the canonical IL-2 signaling threshold of 10 pM.
source: Furthermore, thiss model of IL-2 production predicted a weak antigen dependency that saturated near the canonical IL-2 signaling threshold of 10 pM (Smith, 1988) (Figure 3E), revealing a discrepancy between the established pathway regulation and our experimental results.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the classical model with reference to Figure 3E and citation to Smith, 1988.

claim: IL-2 receptor exposure to 10 pM of IL-2 is biophysically sufficient to trigger ligand binding.
source: IL-2 receptor exposure to only 10 pM of IL-2 is biophysically sufficient to trigger ligand binding (Smith, 1988), and subsequent STAT phosphorylation sharply inhibits IL-2 synthesis (Long and Adler, 2006; Villarino et al., 2007; Waysbort et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Smith, 1988.

claim: STAT phosphorylation sharply inhibits IL-2 synthesis.
source: IL-2 receptor exposure to only 10 pM of IL-2 is biophysically sufficient to trigger ligand binding (Smith, 1988), and subsequent STAT phosphorylation sharply inhibits IL-2 synthesis (Long and Adler, 2006; Villarino et al., 2007; Waysbort et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The classical model predicted [IL-2]max ∝ (NT cells)^(+0.25±0.005) × [Antigen]^(+0.32±0.008).
source: In Figure 3F we show that the two-dimensional fit of the predicted scaling exponents for the classical model(2)[IL−2]maxpredicted∝(NT cells)+0.25(±0.005)×[Antigen]+0.32(±0.008),was also incompatible with our experimental results (Equation 1).
evidence: This is the scaling law predicted by the classical model, explicitly stated with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: The pSTAT5 response was proportional to the product of IL-2Rα abundance and accumulated [IL-2] over time leading up to [IL-2]max.
source: The pSTAT5 response was proportional to the product of IL-2Rα abundance and accumulated [IL-2] over time leading up to [IL-2]max, but the efficiency of STAT5 phosphorylation lessened with increasing antigen dose (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 4A showing the relationship.

claim: The efficiency of STAT5 phosphorylation lessened with increasing antigen dose.
source: The pSTAT5 response was proportional to the product of IL-2Rα abundance and accumulated [IL-2] over time leading up to [IL-2]max, but the efficiency of STAT5 phosphorylation lessened with increasing antigen dose (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 4A showing the antigen-dependent effect.

claim: TCR signaling inhibits the pSTAT5 response to IL-2.
source: This observation is consistent with previous reports of TCR signaling inhibiting the pSTAT5 response to IL-2 (Lee et al., 1999; Yamane et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as consistent with prior literature, with citations to Lee et al., 1999 and Yamane et al., 2005.

claim: The quantity of stimulating antigen did not affect the average EC50 of IL-2 response.
source: Examining the geometric mean of pSTAT5 in activated (IL-2Rα+) T cells, we found that the quantity of stimulating antigen did not affect the average EC50, i.e., sensitivity, of IL-2 response (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 4B showing EC50 measurements.

claim: Increasing antigen dose resulted in higher levels of IL-2 receptors at 48 hr.
source: Instead, we observed that increasing antigen dose resulted in higher levels of IL-2 receptors at 48 hr (Figure 4C), yet paradoxically dampened the amplitude of STAT5 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 4C showing receptor levels.

claim: Increasing antigen dose dampened the amplitude of STAT5 phosphorylation despite higher levels of IL-2 receptors.
source: Instead, we observed that increasing antigen dose resulted in higher levels of IL-2 receptors at 48 hr (Figure 4C), yet paradoxically dampened the amplitude of STAT5 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is directly stated as a paradoxical observation from the data.

claim: Antigen signaling inhibits IL-2 response at the level of STAT5 phosphorylation rather than at the level of IL-2 receptor engagement.
source: Consequently, we postulated that antigen signaling inhibits IL-2 response not at the level of IL-2 receptor engagement, but rather at the level of STAT5 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated as a postulate based on the experimental observations.

claim: TCR-driven inhibition of IL-2 signaling scales linearly with antigen dose when factoring out dynamic variation in IL-2 receptor abundance.
source: By factoring out the dynamic variation in IL-2 receptor abundance associated with T cell activation, CCVA demonstrated that TCR-driven inhibition of IL-2 signaling scales linearly with antigen dose (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 4F showing the linear scaling from CCVA analysis.

claim: The inhibitory effect of TCR on IL-2 signaling decays throughout the course of the T cell response.
source: Furthermore, CCVA showed that this inhibitory effect decays throughout the course of the T cell response (Figure 4G), independently of changes in IL-2 receptor levels.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 4G showing temporal decay.

claim: Titrated antigen-driven inhibition of IL-2 signaling could delay pSTAT5-mediated shutdown of IL-2 production, enabling accumulation of IL-2 beyond 10 pM.
source: We hypothesized that this titrated antigen-driven inhibition of IL-2 signaling could delay pSTAT5-mediated shutdown of IL-2 production, especially in strongly activated cells, thus enabling the accumulation of IL-2 beyond the canonical pSTAT5 signaling threshold of 10 pM (Smith, 1988).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Persistent TCR signaling is required to sustain IL-2 production at all times.
source: We demonstrated that persistent TCR signaling is required to sustain IL-2 production (Huppa et al., 2003) at all times.
evidence: This is stated as demonstrated with citation to Huppa et al., 2003.

claim: Administration of an antibody that disrupted TCR-pMHC contact quickly shut down IL-2 production.
source: Administration of an antibody that disrupted TCR-pMHC contact quickly shut down IL-2 production (Figure 5A–B) and concomitantly increased pSTAT5 within the population (Figure 5C–D), further suggesting inhibition of IL-2 production by pSTAT5 response, and of pSTAT5 by TCR signaling.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 5A-B showing the experimental results.

claim: Disruption of TCR-pMHC contact concomitantly increased pSTAT5 within the population.
source: Administration of an antibody that disrupted TCR-pMHC contact quickly shut down IL-2 production (Figure 5A–B) and concomitantly increased pSTAT5 within the population (Figure 5C–D), further suggesting inhibition of IL-2 production by pSTAT5 response, and of pSTAT5 by TCR signaling.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 5C-D showing the experimental results.

claim: Blocking pSTAT5 via a chemical inhibitor of JAK activity increased the number of IL-2 producing cells.
source: Consistent with reports of negative feedback inhibition of IL-2 production by STAT5-mediated IL-2 signaling (Long and Adler, 2006; Villarino et al., 2007; Waysbort et al., 2013), blocking pSTAT5 via a chemical inhibitor of Janus kinase (JAK) activity increased the number of IL-2 producing cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 5D and citations to prior literature.

claim: Dual inhibition of IL-2 and TCR signaling resulted in a slower decline in IL-2 producers (τdrop = 2.2 ± 0.1 hr) compared to antigen-blocked conditions alone (τdrop = 0.5 ± 0.1 hr).
source: Strikingly, in contrast to the rapid drop (τdrop = 0.5 ± 0.1 hr) observed in antigen-blocked conditions, dual inhibition of IL-2 and TCR signaling resulted in a slower decline in IL-2 producers (τdrop = 2.2 ± 0.1 hr) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific time constants and reference to Figure 5D.

claim: pSTAT5 signaling following antigen withdrawal functions as a swifter mechanism to shut down IL-2 secretion compared to the loss of TCR signal alone.
source: This demonstrates that pSTAT5 signaling following antigen withdrawal functions as a swifter mechanism to shut down IL-2 secretion compared to the loss of TCR signal alone.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The TCR-pSTAT5-IL-2 biochemical network forms a coherent feed forward loop.
source: This biochemical network (Figure 5E) forms a coherent feed forward loop, in which a signal (TCR) and its effect on a target (inhibition of pSTAT5) regulate a common output in the same direction (promoting IL-2 production).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 5E showing the network architecture.

claim: The TCR-pSTAT5-IL-2 network is a type IV coherent feed-forward loop.
source: More specifically, this is a type IV coherent feed-forward loop, where one arm directly promotes an output, and the other arm represses an output's inhibitor (Alon, 2007).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation to Alon, 2007 for the classification.

claim: Type IV coherent feed-forward loops have signal delay properties and mutual exclusion of target and repressor signals.
source: Theoretical studies of such motifs have highlighted their signal delay properties and mutual exclusion of target and repressor signals (Mangan and Alon, 2003), as has been observed for IL-2 and pSTAT5 (Long and Adler, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from theoretical studies with citations.

claim: The coherent feed-forward loop architecture enforces tight synchronization between IL-2 production and sustenance of antigen signaling.
source: Through antigenic control of pSTAT5-mediated repression, IL-2 synthesis is neither terminated before nor extended beyond the loss of antigen signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the functional consequence of the regulatory architecture.

claim: Greater fractions of smaller populations of T cells maintained IL-2 secretion for longer periods of time.
source: Using the cytokine-capture assay, we found that greater fractions of smaller populations of T cells maintained IL-2 secretion for longer periods of time (Figure 6A), consistently with in vivo studies (Sojka et al., 2004).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6A and citation to Sojka et al., 2004.

claim: Smaller populations of T cells (10^3) yielded far fewer IL-2-producing cells than larger populations despite accumulating greater concentrations of IL-2.
source: Paradoxically, though smaller populations of T cells (103) could accumulate greater concentrations of IL-2 ([IL-2]max) than larger populations (Figure 2B,G), they yielded far fewer IL-2-producing cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is directly stated as a paradoxical observation with references to Figures 2B, 2G, and 6B.

claim: Both large and small T cell populations showed similarly limited consumption of human IL-2 before their respective times of maximal mouse IL-2 accumulation.
source: We found that both large and small populations showed similarly limited consumption of hIL-2 before their respective times of maximal mouse IL-2 accumulation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6C showing consumption measurements.

claim: The onset of human IL-2 consumption correlated with high pSTAT5-driven upregulation of IL-2Rα.
source: The onset of hIL-2 consumption correlated with high pSTAT5-driven upregulation of IL-2Rα, which reached its apex several hours after cells amassed maximal mouse IL-2 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6D showing the correlation.

claim: The observed parity in IL-2 accumulation between differently sized T cell populations cannot be attributed to differential cytokine consumption during the IL-2 secretion period.
source: Therefore, the observed parity in IL-2 accumulation between differently sized T cell populations cannot be attributed to differential cytokine consumption during the IL-2 secretion period.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the consumption experiments.

claim: T cells are bimodal in secreting IL-2 at early (<6 hr) timepoints.
source: In previous studies, single-cell measurements established that T cells are bimodal in secreting IL-2 at early (<6 hr) timepoints; stronger antigenic stimuli increases the number of IL-2-producing cells, but not the amount of IL-2 produced per cell (Podtschaske et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies with citations.

claim: Stronger antigenic stimuli increases the number of IL-2-producing cells, but not the amount of IL-2 produced per cell at early timepoints.
source: In previous studies, single-cell measurements established that T cells are bimodal in secreting IL-2 at early (<6 hr) timepoints; stronger antigenic stimuli increases the number of IL-2-producing cells, but not the amount of IL-2 produced per cell (Podtschaske et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies with citations.

claim: Greater antigenic stimulus resulted in larger numbers of IL-2 secreting cells over several days.
source: Our time series experiments did confirm that greater antigenic stimulus resulted in larger numbers of IL-2 secreting cells over several days (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 6E-F showing the data.

claim: The antigen scaling of the number of IL-2 producers was insufficient to account for the observed power law in accumulated IL-2.
source: However, the antigen scaling of the number of IL-2 producers was insufficient to account for the observed power law in accumulated IL-2 (Figure 2F,H).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing the data in Figures 2F, 2H with Figure 6.

claim: A nonlinear relationship emerged between IL-2 concentration and the cumulative number of secreting cells over time.
source: Surprisingly, we observed the emergence of a nonlinear relationship between these two quantities (Figure 7A–B), demonstrating a time-dependent acceleration in the rate of IL-2 production.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 7A-B showing the nonlinear relationship.

claim: At early timepoints (<20 hr) activated T cells secreted IL-2 at similar rates despite different stimulating conditions.
source: Despite different stimulating conditions, at early timepoints (<20 hr) activated T cells secreted IL-2 at similar rates (Figure 7C–D, dashed lines & Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 7C-D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Smaller populations of T cells demonstrated greater time-dependent increases in their rate of IL-2 accumulation per cell (up to 30-fold).
source: However, as smaller populations of T cells sustain longer periods of IL-2 production (Figure 6A), they demonstrated greater time-dependent increases in their rate of IL-2 accumulation per cell (up to 30-fold) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 6A and 7C showing the acceleration.

claim: T cells stimulated with low doses of antigen maintained a constant secretion rate for longer periods of time, slowly building their acceleration in cytokine production.
source: In parallel, T cells stimulated with low doses of antigen maintained a constant secretion rate for longer periods of time, slowly building their acceleration in cytokine production, while strongly-activated T cells increased their apparent secretion rate sooner (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 7D showing the antigen-dependent dynamics.

claim: Strongly-activated T cells increased their apparent secretion rate sooner than weakly-activated T cells.
source: In parallel, T cells stimulated with low doses of antigen maintained a constant secretion rate for longer periods of time, slowly building their acceleration in cytokine production, while strongly-activated T cells increased their apparent secretion rate sooner (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 7D showing the antigen-dependent dynamics.

claim: Time- and antigen-dependent acceleration in the rate of IL-2 secretion amplified the effect of small differences in the duration and amplitude of T cell signaling.
source: This time- and antigen-dependent acceleration in the rate of IL-2 secretion (Figure 7E) amplified the effect of small differences in the duration and amplitude of T cell signaling (Supplement to Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to Figure 7E and Supplement to Figure 7.

claim: Acceleration in IL-2 secretion explained the observed nonlinear kinetics of IL-2 accumulation.
source: It explained the observed nonlinear kinetics of IL-2 accumulation, and underlied the population size-independence of [IL-2]max and its expanded dynamic range.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the observed phenomena.

claim: Acceleration in IL-2 secretion underlied the population size-independence of [IL-2]max and its expanded dynamic range.
source: It explained the observed nonlinear kinetics of IL-2 accumulation, and underlied the population size-independence of [IL-2]max and its expanded dynamic range.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the observed phenomena.

claim: The computational model captured the experimentally observed progression of molecular states within individual T cells.
source: To understand how these newly found regulations contribute to the emergence of the observed IL-2 scaling laws, we employed biochemically explicit computational modeling of the IL-2 pathway to build an ordinary differential equation model (see 'Materials and methods') that captured the experimentally observed progression of molecular states within individual T cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 8A and the Materials and methods section.

claim: The model reproduced the measured dynamics of the IL-2 production pathway for different quantities of antigens and numbers of T cells.
source: While accurately predicting IL-2 consumption will require accounting for cell proliferation and death, which exert stronger effects on longer (>3 day) timescales (Figure 2C), our model reproduces the measured dynamics of the IL-2 production pathway for different quantities of antigens and numbers of T cells (Figures 8C and 9A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 8C and 9A showing model-experiment comparison.

claim: The model recapitulates the scaling law [IL-2]max ∝ (NT cells)^(-0.12±0.03) × (NAntigen)^(+0.82±0.02).
source: Most significantly, it recapitulates the scaling law (Figure 9A bottom):(3)[IL−2]maxmodel∝(NT cells)−0.12(±0.03)×(NAntigen)+0.82(±0.02).
evidence: This is the scaling law from the model, explicitly stated with reference to Figure 9A.

claim: Removing TCR inhibition of pSTAT5 from the model leads to low saturation in [IL-2]max and spurious scaling with NT cell and NAntigen.
source: In Figure 9B, we tested the importance of the TCR-mediated inhibition of IL-2 signaling. Our complete model accounts for the antigen-dependency of pSTAT5 gain with increasing levels of IL-2Rα and IL-2 (Figures 4A and 9B, top). Removing this inhibitory crosstalk eliminates the antigen dose dependency of pSTAT5 response (Figure 9B, middle). It also results in a decreased antigen-dependency of [IL-2]max that flattens at ∼10 pM (Figure 9B, bottom), the classical threshold for STAT5 phosphorylation (Wang and Smith, 1987), and thus for termination of IL-2 production (Long and Adler, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model simulations shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Abrogating the acceleration in IL-2 production prevents small populations of T cells from accumulating comparable amounts of IL-2 to those secreted by larger populations.
source: In contrast, abrogating the acceleration in IL-2 production yields a simple linear correspondence between these variables (Figure 9C, middle), and prevents small populations of T cells from accumulating comparable amounts of IL-2 to those secreted by larger populations.
evidence: This is stated as a result from model simulations shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The lack of acceleration decreases the scaling exponent of [IL-2]max with antigen dose.
source: The lack of acceleration also decreases the scaling exponent of [IL-2]max with antigen dose (Figure 9C, bottom), as the antigen-dependence of IL-2 accumulation is limited to differences in the cumulative number of IL-2 producing cells (Supplement to Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model simulations shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The model forecasted that larger populations of T cells would sustain higher concentrations of IL-2 than smaller populations under JAK inhibition.
source: Moreover, it forecasted that larger populations of T cells would sustain higher concentrations of IL-2 than smaller populations (Figure 9D, top left).
evidence: This is stated as a model prediction shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Experimentally treating cells with a JAK inhibitor confirmed the model's predictions for IL-2 accumulation dynamics.
source: Experimentally treating cells with a JAK inhibitor at time 0 confirmed these predictions, and validated our model's projections for the dynamics of IL-2 accumulation following JAK blockade (Figure 9D, bottom).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 9D showing experimental validation.

claim: The empirical scaling of IL-2 accumulation is critically dependent on feedbacks from IL-2 signaling.
source: These computational and experimental results demonstrate that the empirical scaling of IL-2 accumulation is critically dependent on feedbacks from IL-2 signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the computational and experimental results.

claim: [IL-2]max for a mixed population of T cell clones is determined by the combined antigen doses, independently of cell numbers.
source: The model predicted and experiments confirmed that [IL-2]max for a mixed population of T cell clones is determined by the combined antigen doses, independently of cell numbers (Figure 10A; Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 10A and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: IL-2 is a collective measure of global antigenic load with the potential to coordinate polyclonal responses.
source: This result demonstrates that IL-2 is a collective measure of global antigenic load with the potential to coordinate polyclonal responses.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the two-clone experiments.

claim: Throughout the IL-2 production phase (t < 50 hr), IL-2 produced by 2 clones in the same well is approximately equal to the sum of the IL-2 made by the same two populations in separate wells.
source: Throughout the IL-2 production phase (t < 50 hr, blue lines), the distributions were centered around a ratio of 1, indicating that IL-2 produced by 2 clones in the same well is approximately equal to the sum of the IL-2 made by the same two populations in separate wells.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 10B showing the ratio distributions.

claim: The IL-2 production phase is dictated by a T cell population's TCR stimulation, regardless of other nearby immune reactions.
source: This result suggests that the IL-2 production phase is dictated by a T cell population's TCR stimulation, regardless of other nearby immune reactions.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Each clone's relative antigen dose could be resolved through the shared cytokine environment via proportional inhibition of the IL-2 pathway.
source: Furthermore, the model and experiments both demonstrated that each clone's relative antigen dose could be resolved through the shared cytokine environment via proportional inhibition of the IL-2 pathway (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 10C showing the resolution of relative antigen doses.

claim: The relative doses of antigen signals for 5C.C7 and A1(M) T cells were detectable through their individual responses to shared IL-2.
source: Remarkably, this theoretical expression was confirmed experimentally. The relative doses of antigen signals for 5C.C7 and A1(M) T cells, which are of similarly high quality, were detectable through their individual responses to shared IL-2 (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 10C showing experimental confirmation.

claim: TCR cross-talk inhibition of the IL-2 pathway provides a graded readout of antigen signaling within activated cells with quantitative resolution across a polyclonal system.
source: Accordingly, the signaling crosstalk unraveled in Figure 4 allows a mixed population of T cells to perform both a local (antigen) and a global (cytokine) measurement of collective stimulus through the IL-2 pathway. Furthermore, TCR cross-talk inhibition of the IL-2 pathway provides a graded readout of antigen signaling within activated cells with quantitative resolution across a polyclonal system.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the functional significance of the cross-talk.

claim: The antigen-dependency of SlopeXtalk established a calibration curve to back-calculate fold changes in the antigenic capacity of tumor tissue suspensions.
source: As in Figure 4A, we found inverse proportionality between SlopeXtalk and titrated concentrations of antigenic peptide, which established a calibration curve to back-calculate fold changes in the antigenic capacity of tumor tissue suspensions (Figure 11B, right).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 11B showing the calibration curve.

claim: The calculated amount of antigen signaling experienced by TRP-1 T cells scaled with tumor cellularity.
source: We found that the calculated amount of antigen signaling experienced by TRP-1 T cells scaled with tumor cellularity (Figure 11B, right): larger tumors, which yielded more input cells per normalized volume, induced greater suppression of IL-2 signaling, and were thus estimated to have a proportionally greater antigen load (inset).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 11B showing the scaling with cellularity.

claim: Antigen presentation per cell did not depend on tumor size.
source: Normalizing the antigen calculated for each tissue source by the number of cells plated, we confirmed that both tumor dilution strategies yielded very similar estimates of antigen presentation per cell, which did not depend on tumor size (Figure 11D, green and red).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 11D showing independence from tumor size.

claim: The antigen presented per cell in the draining lymph nodes scaled with tumor size.
source: Strikingly, our measurements showed that the antigen presented per cell in the draining lymph nodes did scale with tumor size (Figure 11D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 11D showing the scaling.

claim: Scalable inhibition of the IL-2 pathway can resolve a wide dynamic range of antigen quantities.
source: In sum, scalable inhibition of the IL-2 pathway can resolve a wide dynamic range of antigen quantities.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the tumor antigenicity measurements.

claim: A single snapshot measurement of the amplitude of pSTAT5 response to high dose IL-2 can distinguish relative strengths of TCR signaling among activated T cells.
source: This inhibitory cross-talk underlies the [IL-2]max scaling presented in Figure 2, but can be captured with far fewer timepoints; in fact, a single snapshot measurement of the amplitude of pSTAT5 response to high dose IL-2 can distinguish relative strengths of TCR signaling among activated T cells (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Time integration of IL-2 regulatory loops generates collective-level outputs that reflect global antigen abundance with higher fidelity, functional range and temporal persistence than early activation responses.
source: Hence, time integration of IL-2 regulatory loops generates collective-level outputs that reflect global antigen abundance with higher fidelity, functional range and temporal persistence than early activation responses (Figure 1) (Cheong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to Figure 1 and citation to Cheong et al., 2011.

claim: Feedback-controlled, titrated accumulation of IL-2 may help scale and direct the long-term responses of activated cells according their degree of antigenic stimulus.
source: This feedback-controlled, titrated accumulation of IL-2 may help scale and direct the long-term responses of activated cells according their degree of antigenic stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about the functional significance.

claim: IL-2 signaling critically optimizes lymphocyte differentiation, proliferation, and survival.
source: IL-2 signaling critically optimizes lymphocyte differentiation, proliferation, and survival (Williams et al., 2006; Bachmann et al., 2007; Pipkin et al., 2010; Liao et al., 2011; McNally et al., 2011; Boyman and Sprent, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Sustained IL-2-driven IL-2Rα expression corresponds to the adoption of short-lived effector, rather than memory, fates in CD8+ T cells.
source: In the case of in vivo CD8+ T cell differentiation, sustained IL-2-driven IL-2Rα expression corresponds to the adoption of short-lived effector, rather than memory, fates (Kalia et al., 2010; Obar et al., 2010; Pipkin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior studies.

claim: The tight correlation between antigen load and IL-2 accumulation may ensure that large pathogenic challenges are communicated through large IL-2 availability to generate robust effector responses.
source: The tight correlation we find between antigen load and IL-2 accumulation may ensure that large pathogenic challenges are communicated through large IL-2 availability to generate robust effector responses.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about the functional significance.

claim: The expression of IL-2Rα at day four post-infection scales with antigenic affinity, and correlates to greater effector cell expansion and survival.
source: Indeed, another in vivo study has shown that the expression of IL-2Rα at day four post-infection scales with antigenic affinity, and correlates to greater effector cell expansion and survival (Zehn et al., 2009; Kalia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Zehn et al., 2009 and Kalia et al., 2010.

claim: Graded inhibition of pSTAT5 by TCR signaling may directly influence CD4+ T helper subtype differentiation by blocking time-sensitive cytokine signals.
source: Finally, graded inhibition of pSTAT5 by TCR signaling may directly influence CD4+ T helper subtype differentiation by blocking time-sensitive cytokine signals (Yamane and Paul, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citation to Yamane and Paul, 2012.

claim: Positive and negative feedback loops within proximal TCR signaling generate a sharp digital activation filter that is necessary for efficient discrimination of antigenic ligands.
source: Positive and negative feedback loops within proximal TCR signaling generate a sharp digital activation filter that is necessary for efficient discrimination of antigenic ligands (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Das et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior studies.

claim: Binary single parameter readouts are prone to saturation of input detection range, exhibit narrow output dynamic ranges, are subject to shifts in value by cellular death and migration, and provide little information on the functional capacity of activated cells.
source: Such 'percent activated' measurements have been fruitfully used to survey tissue antigenicity (Badovinac and Harty, 2002; Nandi et al., 2009), but binary single parameter readouts carry some limitations: they are prone to saturation of input detection range, exhibit narrow output dynamic ranges, are subject to shifts in value by cellular death and migration, and provide little information on the functional capacity of activated cells.
evidence: This is stated as a critique of binary readouts with citations to prior studies.

claim: Quantifying the degree of TCR-driven inhibition of pSTAT5 signaling inside activated T cells provides an indication of the strength of signaling within the responding population.
source: In contrast, quantifying the degree of TCR-driven inhibition of pSTAT5 signaling inside activated T cells provides an indication of the strength of signaling within the responding population.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the utility of the cross-talk measurement.

claim: Convolution of antigen-dependent STAT5 phosphorylation efficiency with its consequent scaling of IL-2 production increases output resolution of the initiating antigen load.
source: While these measurements are not immune to saturation, convolution of antigen-dependent STAT5 phosphorylation efficiency with its consequent scaling of IL-2 production (Figures 4A, 10C, 11) increases output resolution of the initiating antigen load.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with references to Figures 4A, 10C, and 11.
